articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter-Narcotics and Cyber-Related Designations, Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter-narcotics and cyber-related illicit activities. This action underscores the U.S. government's ongoing commitment to disrupting global criminal networks that pose a threat to national security.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued an Illicit Drugs General License, providing specific authorizations related to certain transactions. Additionally, an amended Russia-related General License was published, alongside updated Frequently Asked Questions, to provide further guidance on existing sanctions programs.

These measures aim to enhance the effectiveness of U.S. sanctions by targeting key facilitators of illicit trade and cybercrime, while also ensuring that legitimate humanitarian and other authorized activities can continue under appropriate licenses.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities and Individuals in Counter-Terrorism Action
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new counter-terrorism designations on November 18, 2026. These actions target individuals and entities identified as supporting terrorist organizations and their activities globally.
The designations aim to disrupt financial networks and logistical support structures that enable terrorist groups to operate, thereby mitigating threats to international security.

Further details regarding the specific individuals and entities designated were made available on the Treasury Department's website, emphasizing the U.S. government's continued efforts to combat terrorism through financial sanctions.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Dual Counter-Narcotics and Counter-Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a dual action on November 13, 2026, implementing designations under both its counter-narcotics and counter-terrorism sanctions programs. This move targets illicit networks involved in both drug trafficking and the financing of terrorism.
These designations aim to sever the financial lifelines of criminal organizations that often engage in a nexus of illicit activities, highlighting the interconnected nature of global threats.
The Treasury Department continues to leverage its sanctions authorities to combat these multifaceted threats, working to protect the U.S. financial system from abuse by malicious actors.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Update to Iran Designation List
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) published an update to its Iran designation list on November 9, 2026. This action reflects the ongoing U.S. policy of applying economic pressure on the Iranian regime.

The update includes modifications to existing listings and may involve the addition of new individuals or entities found to be supporting Iran's destabilizing activities, including its nuclear program, ballistic missile development, and support for terrorism.
These measures are part of a broader strategy to compel Iran to cease its illicit activities and comply with international norms.

articles.headline: U.S. Sanctions Cripple Financial Networks Sustaining the Iranian Regime
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a new round of Iran-related designations on November 6, 2026. These sanctions target financial networks identified as providing substantial support to the Iranian regime.
The action aims to further restrict Iran's access to the international financial system and limit its ability to fund activities deemed destabilizing to regional and global security.
These designations are part of an intensified pressure campaign, building on previous measures to disrupt Iran's illicit financial operations and its various malign activities.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / U.S. Department of State

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Cyber-Related and Transnational Criminal Organization Designations, Expands Cuba Sanctions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on November 5, 2026, targeting cyber-related illicit activities and transnational criminal organizations. Concurrently, OFAC also issued new Cuba designations and published a Cuba-related determination.
The Cuba-related determination extends Executive Order 14404 to four additional sectors of the Cuban economy: manufacturing, technology, electronics, and marine.
This expansion allows the U.S. government to block the property of non-U.S. persons operating in these newly designated sectors, further tightening economic pressure on the Cuban regime.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian Entities, Updates Listings, and Amends Venezuela General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 4, 2026, alongside updates to certain existing Iran-related listings.

In a related action, OFAC published an Iran-related alert, likely pertaining to sanctions evasion tactics, and issued an amended Venezuela-related General License with accompanying Frequently Asked Questions.
These measures reflect the U.S. government's continued focus on countering Iranian illicit activities and providing clarity on sanctions compliance for Venezuela-related transactions.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / U.S. Department of State

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026. This amendment provides updated guidance and authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran.

General Licenses are often issued to clarify the scope of sanctions programs and to permit specific activities that would otherwise be prohibited, typically for humanitarian or other policy-driven reasons.
Entities engaging in Iran-related transactions are advised to review the amended General License carefully to ensure ongoing compliance with U.S. sanctions regulations.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo-Related Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 28, 2026, targeting entities and individuals connected to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
The North Korea designations are part of ongoing efforts to counter Pyongyang's illicit weapons programs and revenue generation activities, which often involve overseas workers and cyber operations.

The Democratic Republic of the Congo-related designations likely address issues such as human rights abuses, corruption, or the exploitation of natural resources, aligning with broader U.S. foreign policy objectives in the region.

articles.headline: EU Imposes Sweeping Sanctions on Russian Banks, Shadow Fleet, and E-commerce
body: The Council of the European Union approved a new package of sanctions against Russia on November 16, 2026, targeting 12 individuals and 101 entities for their role in financing the war against Ukraine.
The new measures include sanctions against 49 Russian banks and financial institutions, major oil refineries, and online marketplaces.

The EU also targeted 15 companies for owning, managing, financing, or insuring tankers in Russia's 'shadow fleet,' and a Singaporean fintech company, ALT Capital PTE Ltd, for facilitating sanctions circumvention.
articles.source: Council of the European Union / European Pravda

articles.headline: EU Sanctions 30 Individuals and Two Entities for Russian FIMI and Cyber Activities
body: The Council of the European Union decided on November 16, 2026, to add 30 individuals and two entities to its list of those subject to EU restrictive measures due to Russia's foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI) and malicious cyber activities.

Among the newly listed entities is the Social Design Agency (SDA), a Moscow-based public relations and political technology company accused of carrying out large-scale information manipulation projects funded and supervised by the Russian Presidential Administration.
These sanctions aim to counter Russia's hybrid activities against third countries and international organizations, with those designated facing asset freezes and travel bans.

articles.headline: UN Security Council Renews Yemen Sanctions, Expands Maritime Oversight
body: The United Nations Security Council unanimously adopted Resolution 2837 (2026) on November 12, 2026, renewing targeted asset freezes and travel bans under the Yemen sanctions regime until November 14, 2027.

The resolution also extends the mandate of the Yemen Panel of Experts until December 15, 2027, and expands the panel to include dedicated maritime security expertise to monitor suspected arms shipments.

The Council urged Member States to strengthen intelligence-sharing and cooperation to prevent weapons and related components from reaching the Houthis, particularly in the Red Sea, Gulf of Aden, and Bab al-Mandab Strait.
articles.source: UN Meetings Coverage and Press Releases / ZIGRAM

articles.headline: UN Security Council Committee Amends One Entry on DPRK Sanctions List
body: On November 13, 2026, the Security Council Committee established pursuant to resolution 1718 (2006) enacted amendments to one entry on its Sanctions List of individuals and entities related to the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK).

The amendment specifically concerns the 'Mansudae Overseas Project Group of Companies,' also known as 'Mansudae Art Studio,' which has been designated for engaging in the exportation of workers from the DPRK to generate revenue for the government.
This update reflects the ongoing international efforts to monitor and enforce sanctions against North Korea's illicit activities, particularly those generating funds for its weapons programs.

articles.headline: BIS Imposes New Export Controls on Remote Access to Advanced AI Chips and Rescinds AI Diffusion Rule
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) published an interim final rule on November 19, 2026, establishing new export licensing requirements for remote access to and exports of advanced-node integrated circuits (AI chips).

The rule creates new end-use restrictions, requiring a license to export, reexport, or transfer AI chips to any country if the exporter has 'knowledge' that the item is destined for a data center providing access to significant compute capacity to entities headquartered in Country Group D:5 (including China) or Macau.

Additionally, the rule imposes a new destination-based license requirement for exports of advanced computing items to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil, and formally rescinds the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule.

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
